newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian leaders pay tribute to China's Deng.
newsitem.headline: Asian leaders pay tribute to China's Deng.

text.p: Asian leaders on Thursday mourned the death of Chinese patriarch Deng Xiaoping and said his reforms transforming China into an economic powerhouse had earned him a place among the world's great statesmen.

From Pakistan to New Zealand, prime ministers and presidents heaped tribute upon Deng, saying he would long be remembered for dismantling the socialist shackles that hobbled China's vast population for decades.
His death at the age 92 marked the end of an era, they said.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he was filled with great sadness at Deng's death and hoped his passing would not affect crucial Japanese-Sino relations, which he said were of growing importance for peace and stability of the world.
"I will continue to work with China's leaders for the long-term stability of our bilateral relationship," Hashimoto said in a statement.

NHK Television quoted Foreign Ministry officials as saying Tokyo did not expect major political or economic changes within China because the political structure around President Jiang Zemin was stable and economic reforms were under way.

Deng, who died late on Wednesday of respiratory failure, introduced economic reforms in 1978, declaring "to get rich is glorious" -- strange words then in the huge socialist nation. His reforms helped open China to the world and deliver year-on-year economic growth of more than nine percent since 1978.
South Korean President Kim Young-sam said he was saddened but hoped Seoul's friendly ties with Beijing would strengthen.
Kim sent a telegram to Jiang and Deng's family, hailing the late leader as "an outstanding political leader who opened a new chapter in world history".
Communist North Korea's de facto leader Kim Jong-il praised Deng as an "intimate friend and comrade-in-arms" of the Korean people and said his death was a great loss to them.

"I, in the name of...the entire Korean people and in my own, extend deep condolences to you and...to the government of the People's Republic of China, the fraternal Chinese people and the bereaved family," the official Korea Central News Agency (KCNA) quoted Kim Jong-il as saying in a message to Jiang.
President Suharto of Indonesia said economic reforms carried out by Deng had benefited China's 1.2 billion people.
India's Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral praised Deng for helping to improve ties between the two Asian giants.
"He not only shaped the destiny of his nation but contributed directly to building good relations," Gujral said.
Pakistani leaders mourned Deng as a great statesman and friend of Pakistan whose death had ended an era.

"His demise represents the passing away of an era. We in Pakistan share the grief of the great Chinese people. (He) will be remembered as a trusted friend of Pakistan," President Farooq Leghari said in a message to Jiang Zemin.
Philippine President Fidel Ramos said Deng opened China to the world and brought modernisation and prosperity.
"The admirable achievements of Deng Xiaoping shaped a new China," he said.
Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said Deng brought about the greatest economic revolution in history that had also affected the lives of others in Asia.
Deng was a great world leader who "saw events in historical sweep, and thought in terms of generations", Goh said.
Malaysia's parliamentary opposition leader, Lim Kit Siang, said: "With the death of Deng Xiaoping, a star has fallen in the international firmament marking the end of an era."
Officials in the British colony of Hong Kong, which reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30, paid their respects.
Colonial Governor Chris Patten was one of the first to be escorted inside the Xinhua news agency, Beijing's de facto mission in Hong Kong, to offer his condolences.
"He will be regarded by future generations as an historic figure," said Patten, the territory's last governor.

Patten was followed by the man who will step into his shoes when the colony is handed over to China. Future leader Tung Chee-hwa, flanked by members of his inner cabinet, bowed three times to a large black and white photograph of Deng.

Taiwan's Presidential Office sent its condolences to Deng's family and urged a "peaceful, cooperative, prosperous new era" between Taipei and Beijing. But the island, which Beijing regards as a renegade province, maintained a military alert and urged calm.
Vietnam's communist government, which fought a bloody border war with Beijing during the late 1970s, offered formal but brief condolences.
But reaction was not all praise.
Tibet's government-in-exile accused Deng of decades of repression and said his death offered a chance to his successor to solve the region's longstanding problems.
The government-in-exile of the troubled Himalayan region, headed by spiritual leader the Dalai Lama, said he was "directly responsible for decades of repression and suffering in Tibet".
